Right: the same graph with the edge between C and D reversed (in the accent color); no arrow enters D any more, so has_path() returns False." width="100%"} Returns `True` if `target=` can be reached from `source=` by following edges, in their direction on a directed graph. This is a plain reachability test: it stops as soon as the target is found and ignores edge weights, so it is cheaper than computing a shortest path when only the yes/no answer matters. Every node has a path to itself. On an undirected graph, `has_path(u, v)` is `True` exactly when `u` and `v` are in the same connected component. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The starting node, as an integer ID or a string label. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The destination node, as an integer ID or a string label. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if a path exists, otherwise `False`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a label does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a directed chain, every node can reach the nodes downstream of it, but not the ones upstream: ::: {#abe950ae .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) graph.has_path("A", "C"), graph.has_path("C", "A"), graph.has_path("A", "D") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, False, False) ``` ::: :::
